components.text: Whether the cosmological cause supplies grounds for a morally good rather than morally unspecified creator.
Whether Craig's separate moral argument can provide the missing asymmetry in the creator's character.
The cosmological inference does not identify the transcendent creator's moral character.
The separate moral argument is the proposed source of an asymmetry favoring goodness.
Whether an independent moral asymmetry justifies treating abundant suffering differently from abundant goodness.
Whether a morally neutral creator conclusion can itself break the good-creator and evil-creator symmetry.
Whether specifically Christian historical evidence independently outweighs the observational parity challenge.
Craig must establish a relevant moral asymmetry rather than merely posit a good creator.
Morally neutral creator evidence cannot by itself block observational exclusion of either moral extreme.
Whether apparently gratuitous suffering makes it probable that God has no morally sufficient reasons.
Whether merely possible unknown purposes establish a relevant asymmetry from the evil-creator case.
The evidential inference requires probability that God lacks morally sufficient reasons for permitting suffering.
A better world must be genuinely feasible given providential purposes, not merely imaginable.
Whether observational parity applies when divine goodness is not inferred inductively from worldly goods.
Whether the concrete mirrored theodicies remain equally effective for an evil creator.
Whether changing the label from evil God to evil creator resolves the evidential symmetry.
An evil creator is not worship-worthy and therefore is not literally God under Craig's definition.
Divine goodness is not inferred merely by counting worldly goods.
The observational parity still requires an evidential asymmetry rather than a terminological distinction.
Whether the suffering objection depends on the atheist affirming objective evil or moral realism.
The suffering argument need not assert objective evil or accept moral realism.
Apparently excessive suffering can ground a probabilistic challenge without an objective-evil premise.
Whether objective moral values exist and, if so, whether their existence requires God.
Whether suffering instead supplies counterevidence against the proposed moral foundation.
Neither objective morality nor its alleged dependence on God has been adequately established.
The observed suffering may function as counterevidence within Craig's own moral premises.
Whether apparently baffling testimony discriminates resurrection from the baseline occurrence of hard-to-explain reports.
Baffling testimony must discriminate against the baseline expectation that some such reports arise naturally.
Whether atheism offers an adequate grounding account for objective moral values and duties.
Whether the suffering argument can proceed without objective morality.
Theism offers a transcendent explanation for objective moral status while Law supplies no alternative account.
The internal suffering argument does not itself answer the metaphysical grounding question.
Whether the resurrection case has discriminatory explanatory features beyond being merely baffling testimony.
The resurrection claim must be compared by explanatory criteria and assessed in its distinctive religious-historical context.
Whether a transcendent creator conclusion establishes the perfect goodness required by Craig's God.
Whether the separate moral argument can provide the missing grounds for goodness.
Whether God's nature and commands independently resolve cosmological moral neutrality.
Even a successful cosmological argument would establish no preference between a good and evil creator.
Calling an evil creator nondivine does not add evidence for the creator's goodness.
A separate moral argument, not cosmology, must carry the moral-character inference.
Whether the cosmological conclusion supplies any basis for the creator's perfect goodness.
The cosmological case is deductive and cannot be answered merely by professing ignorance about origins.
Its deductive form still does not determine the cause's moral character.
Whether humans can reliably assign probabilities that observed goods or evils are gratuitous under omniscient providence.
Whether apparently excessive suffering supports a reliable likelihood judgment against a good God.
Whether the same skeptical limit equally protects an evil creator from abundant goodness.
Finite observers cannot reliably judge whether apparent goods or evils are gratuitous within omniscient providence.
The probability inference from apparently gratuitous suffering depends on cognitive access to divine purposes.
The same skeptical limit appears applicable to judgments about gratuitous good under an evil creator.
Whether observers can know that particular suffering lacks a morally sufficient long-range providential purpose.
Whether long-range ignorance creates a relevant asymmetry rather than equally protecting an evil creator.
Long-range consequences may conceal morally sufficient reasons for particular suffering.
Hidden historical consequences do not by themselves establish an asymmetry between good and evil creators.
